e.t: This adjective means “good.” It describes something viewed positively—whether a person, thing, action, or condition—and can express what is beneficial, desirable, or morally sound when the surrounding passage makes that aspect clear. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 495 times, showing a broad and frequent use rather than a term limited to one subject. Its precise force depends on what it describes.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person called “Addai” or “Aththe.” It is not a common noun describing an object, action, or quality, but a personal designation. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 12:16. The available information identifies the name and its single occurrence, but does not provide surrounding verse text or further details about the person. Its precise significance in that passage therefore depends on the wider context of Nehemiah 12.

This word is a proper name rendered “Addō” or “Aththo.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears six times across six verses, in 2 Chronicles, Ezra, and Zechariah. The name occurs in passages associated with different individuals named Addō, so the surrounding verse is needed to identify which person is intended. Its basic function remains that of a personal name.

This verb describes becoming numb or losing normal sensation, expressed by the meanings “become dumb” and “become tingly.” It refers to a change in bodily feeling or ability, rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs twice, both times in Jeremiah 38:29–30. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is becoming numb or becoming unable to speak.

This word means “truth”: what is genuine, reliable, and faithful to reality. It is a noun used to speak of truth as a quality or reality rather than simply describing something as true. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings, it occurs 149 times, showing that truth is a recurring scriptural concern. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding words, but its central meaning remains truth—what can be trusted rather than falsehood or deception.

Alōēs; Alis is a proper name belonging to a person mentioned in the Greek Old Testament. As a name, it identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, object, or general idea. This word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Nehemiah 10:25. The available information establishes the name and its use as a personal designation, but it does not provide the surrounding verse text or enough context to explain anything further about the person. Its precise significance in that passage therefore depends on reading the surrounding context.

This word means “amen”: an interjection used as a brief, affirmative response. It expresses agreement with, or confirmation of, what has been said, prayed, or proclaimed. In the Greek Septuagint corpus represented here, it occurs five times—three times in Old Testament books and twice in deuterocanonical books. Its repeated rendering as “Amen” preserves the same concise expression rather than translating it into a longer phrase.

This Greek LXX verb means “lead up” or “head up”—to bring or guide someone or something upward or toward a higher place. Its basic sense focuses on upward movement under someone’s direction. It occurs 106 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings of this corpus, so its exact expression can depend on what is being led or brought up in a sentence. As a verb, it describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality.

This Greek LXX noun means “bringing up” or “raising up.” It describes the act of lifting, bringing something forward, or causing it to rise. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, at Genesis 50:24. Its basic meaning remains broad because the surrounding verse text is not included, so the precise object or action must be understood from that passage. As a noun, it names the act or process itself rather than functioning as a command or description of a person.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “answer”—a reply given in response to a question, challenge, or statement. It presents the idea of responding rather than speaking without a prompt. In the Septuagint, it occurs twice, both times in Job, showing a focused use rather than a broadly repeated term. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and conversation, but its central meaning remains a spoken or expressed reply.

This noun refers to “what is moved” or “baggage”—the belongings or load carried from one place to another. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used six times, including passages describing Israel’s movements and possessions. The word therefore points to movable goods rather than a person or fixed place. Its exact reference may vary with the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains something transported, carried, or taken along.

This verb means “shut up”: to close something or keep it from being open or accessible. It describes an action of blocking or enclosing, rather than merely stopping speech. In the Greek LXX, it occurs 27 times across the Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing repeated use for closing or restricting access in different passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being closed or confined there.

This word describes someone or something as “senseless”—without sound judgment or understanding. It can function as an adjective describing a person or thing, and as a noun referring to a senseless person. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures represented in this LXX corpus, it occurs 132 times, especially in wisdom writings such as Proverbs and Ecclesiastes. The word commonly marks a lack of good sense, rather than merely a temporary mistake. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word is a proper name rendered “Batharōth” or “Vatharoth.” It identifies a named place in the Greek Old Testament wording of Joshua 19:6. Because it appears only once in the LXX corpus, its meaning is limited to this geographic name rather than a general idea, action, or quality. The two renderings are name variants, not separate concepts within this usage.

Baitharan, also rendered Vetharan, is a proper name rather than a descriptive word. It identifies a named person, place, or other specific entity in the Greek Old Testament text; the available lexical information does not specify which kind. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Numbers 32:36. Its precise referent is therefore determined by the surrounding verse and passage, not by the name alone.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Balaa” or “Valaa.” It identifies a particular named person, place, or other entity rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles. The available references establish its use as a name, but without the surrounding verse text they do not determine the exact referent in each occurrence. Its precise identification therefore depends on the genealogical or listing context of those passages.

This word is a proper name: “Beselēl” or “Veselil.” It functions as a personal name rather than a general description, so its meaning is chiefly the person designated by that name. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Ezra 10:30. Without the verse text, the name itself does not provide additional information about that person’s role or the surrounding event.

This Greek LXX verb means “shower” or “rain,” describing water falling from the sky. It can refer to ordinary rainfall or to a significant downpour, depending on the surrounding passage. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in passages from Genesis through Amos. Its central idea remains the act of rain falling, whether presented as a needed provision or as part of a powerful event. The exact force in any verse depends on its immediate context.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Gaibenenom; Yevenenom.” It identifies a particular named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general category. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 28:3. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text or a broader lexical definition, its exact identity and role must be determined from that passage’s context.

This adjective describes someone as talkative or babbling—speaking freely or excessively, without necessarily implying that the speech is wise or helpful. It can describe a person marked by many words rather than quiet restraint. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, appearing in Psalms, Proverbs, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and the person being described.

This noun means “standing aloof” or “separation”—being apart rather than joined together. It can describe a state of distance or withdrawal. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 3:7; the precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains separation: a condition in which people or things stand apart.

This word means “teacher”—a person who instructs or guides others in learning. As a noun, it identifies the person rather than the act of teaching. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Esther and once in 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on someone who provides instruction, while the surrounding passage determines what is being taught and how the person’s role is being presented.

This noun refers to prepared hide or tanned skin—animal skin treated so it could be used as a durable material. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 39:20. The word identifies the material itself rather than an action or quality, but the surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly how that material is being used there. Its basic meaning remains a worked, usable skin prepared for a practical purpose.

This Greek LXX adverb means “strongly” or “mightily,” describing how an action is carried out. It adds the idea of power, force, or great strength to the verb it modifies, rather than naming a person or thing. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus: once in 1 Chronicles and once in Wisdom. In both places, it is rendered “mightily,” supporting the sense of acting with notable strength or power. Its exact emphasis in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “receive”: to take something or someone in as accepted or given. It describes the act of receiving rather than naming the thing received. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 19 times, so its central meaning remains consistent across several passages. The word appears in contexts ranging from God receiving people to people receiving what is given. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is received, but the basic action is acceptance or taking in.

This verb means “strip off the skin from.” It describes the physical act of removing an outer skin or hide from something. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, so it is a specific action word rather than a broad term for general removal. Its exact force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains the removal of skin from an animal or other object. The word functions as a verb, expressing what someone does.

Ekkas is a proper name, referring to a person named Ekkas rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 2 Samuel 23:26. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not provide additional meaning or an explanation of the person’s role. Its significance in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and narrative context.

This Greek LXX verb means “flow out”: it describes something moving outward from a source, usually as a liquid or stream. It is a word of outward movement rather than simply existing or remaining in place. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, including passages in Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and 1 Maccabees. Its exact force—what is flowing and from where—depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains movement outward or away from a source.

This Greek LXX verb means “drive” or “row”: it describes causing something to move, especially by directing it forward or propelling it through water. The same basic word can therefore describe movement by a driver or movement by a rower, depending on the sentence. It occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, across passages from Exodus, Kings, Isaiah, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on what or whom the sentence says is being moved.

This noun means “coil”: something wound or arranged in a circular or spiral form. It names a physical shape rather than an action, person, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, at Genesis 49:11. Because the surrounding verse text is not included, the word’s precise role in that passage must be understood from its context, but its basic lexical sense remains a coil or winding shape.

Eliphalias, also rendered Elifalias, is a proper name referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 15:21. The name itself does not provide a broader definition or explain the person’s character; its specific significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

The word is a proper name, appearing as “Emekraphain” or “Emekrafen.” It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it occurs once, in Joshua 18:16. The name itself does not explain the entity’s location or role; those details must be understood from the surrounding passage in Joshua. Its spelling may appear differently in English transliteration, but both supplied forms represent this same biblical name.

e.h: Binding In or Being in Need
e.t: This Greek LXX verb expresses being bound in or being in need. It can describe something held or enclosed, and it can also describe a condition of lacking what is needed. Thus, its basic idea may concern either binding or need, depending on how it functions in the sentence. It occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, with occurrences from Exodus through Sirach.

gl: with water in it; holding water
d: with water in it; holding water

e.t: This adjective describes something that has water in it or is capable of holding water. It points to a water-containing quality rather than naming the water itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, showing a specific descriptive use rather than a broad range of meanings. Its exact force in any sentence depends on the thing being described, but the central idea remains something filled with, supplied with, or retaining water.

This Greek LXX verb means “spend entirely”: to use something up completely, leaving nothing remaining. It describes complete expenditure or consumption rather than merely using part of what is available. The word occurs 27 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, including passages from Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being exhausted and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “overflow”: to flow over a boundary or spread beyond what can contain it. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, including passages from Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one verse depends on what is said to overflow and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is movement that exceeds its limits.

This word means “700,” or seven hundred. It is an adjective used to describe a quantity, number, or counted group. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 40 times, showing a recurring numerical use rather than a rare or specialized expression. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: it identifies an amount consisting of seven hundred. The surrounding noun or statement determines what is being counted, while the number itself contributes the precise quantity.

This noun refers to an inventor or discoverer—someone who finds, develops, or brings something previously unknown or unmade to light. It describes a person by what he originates or uncovers, rather than an action or object itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Proverbs and once in 2 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls more on creating something new or discovering something hidden.

This noun means “fashion,” naming a way something is presented or arranged. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs only once, at 4 Maccabees 6:2. Because no verse text or surrounding passage is provided, its particular force in that sentence cannot be explained further. Its basic lexical sense remains “fashion”: a noun naming what is presented in that manner.

This Greek LXX adjective means “well-named” or “southerly.” It describes something recognized by a good or fitting name, or something located toward the south. The word functions as a description rather than naming an action. It occurs 18 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing mainly in Old Testament books with one deuterocanonical occurrence. The surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is on being well-named or on a southern position or direction.

Zanō, also rendered Zano, is a proper name rather than a word describing a quality, action, or object. It functions as a specific name in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs twice in the LXX corpus, in 1 Chronicles 4:18 and Nehemiah 3:13. Without the surrounding verse text, the available information identifies the name itself but does not establish whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity.

Ἤρ is a proper name, referring to a person named Er, also rendered Ir. It is not a general word describing an object, action, or quality, but a personal name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament, across eight verses, from Genesis through 1 Chronicles. Because a name identifies someone rather than states a definition, its meaning is primarily the person it names; the surrounding passage is needed to identify which Er is intended in a particular reference.

Themad is a proper name, also rendered “Themath.” It identifies a particular person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Isaiah 37:12. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the specific person or place identified by the name cannot be described further from this word alone. Its meaning is therefore its identity as a proper name, with “Themath” serving as an alternate supplied rendering.

This noun means “divine reverence; awe of God.” It describes deep respect directed toward God, recognizing him as worthy of reverence. The word appears seven times across seven verses in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding words and subject, but its central meaning remains reverent awe directed toward God.

This Greek LXX adjective means “of summer.” It describes something belonging to, associated with, or characteristic of the summer season, functioning as a descriptive word rather than naming a person or object by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times across three verses. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the noun or situation it describes, but its basic sense remains seasonal: something connected with summer.

Thoou is a proper name, referring to a person named Thoou or Thou. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both times in 2 Samuel 8:9–10. Because the word functions as a name rather than a descriptive term, its basic meaning is the identification of that person, not a quality or action. The precise role of the person in those verses depends on the surrounding passage and the verse text.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Iedida,” also rendered “Iethitha.” It functions as a personal designation rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 22:1. The name’s specific significance or role cannot be established from the name alone; the surrounding verse and passage provide that information.

Iezichar, also rendered Iezikhar, is a proper personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears once, at 2 Kings 12:22. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the person’s role or significance there. Its meaning as used in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding biblical context.

This verb means to drive horses or to drive a chariot. It describes the action of directing horses while riding or controlling a horse-drawn vehicle. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ezekiel 23, so its use is limited to those two passages rather than broadly distributed across the Greek Old Testament. The word itself points to skilled movement and control involving horses or a chariot, while the surrounding verse determines the specific scene in which the action appears.

Kaathi is a proper name, preserved as “Kaathi,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in Numbers 26:57 and once in 1 Chronicles 6:39. These references identify where the name appears, but the available information does not provide the surrounding verse text or additional meaning beyond its use as a personal or group name.

This adjective describes someone or something as using “bad arts,” referring to methods or skills marked as bad. It characterizes how an action is carried out rather than naming a person, object, or event by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the use of bad methods or practices.

This noun means “smoke”: the visible cloud or vapor produced when something burns. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for smoke as a physical feature associated with fire, rising, spreading, or filling the air. Because the word occurs 28 times across the Greek Old Testament corpus, it is a normal descriptive term rather than a rare technical expression. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains smoke—the substance seen drifting from burning material or fire.

This verb means to leave someone or something behind, or to remain when others have gone. It can describe separation, what is left over, or continued presence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 272 times, showing broad use for both leaving and remaining across many kinds of situations. Its basic meaning is determined by whether the sentence focuses on what someone departs from or on what continues afterward.

This verb means “pour over,” describing liquid being poured onto or across something. It presents the act of directing a substance outward rather than merely holding or carrying it. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, with its use spread across Genesis, Job, Psalms, and 4 Maccabees. The exact force in any verse depends on what is being poured and the surrounding sentence.

This word means “mirror,” referring to an object used to see a reflection. It is a noun naming the reflective object itself, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Exodus 38:26. The precise significance of the mirror in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word’s ordinary meaning remains a mirror or reflective surface.

This word means “muzzle,” the noun for an object placed over an animal’s mouth. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: in Psalm 31:9 and twice in Ezekiel 19:4 and 19:9. Its basic sense is concrete and specific: it names the muzzle itself rather than an action or a quality. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain how the object or image functions in each passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “bend” or “tip over.” It describes an action in which something is turned from an upright or straight position, whether by bending it or causing it to fall to one side. The word appears 51 times in the Greek LXX, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is used repeatedly in different passages. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being bent or tipped and the surrounding sentence.

Maidaba, also rendered Methava, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place or location in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs twice in the LXX corpus, in Joshua 13:9 and 1 Chronicles 19:7. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise role in each passage cannot be described further, but its basic meaning is the place-name itself.

Marron is a proper name, represented as “Marrōn” or “Marron,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. Its function is to identify a named figure or entity within the Greek Old Testament text. It occurs four times in the Greek Joshua, in Joshua 11 and 12. The available references establish its repeated use there, while the name itself does not carry an additional ordinary definition.

This Greek LXX noun means “singing; chanting.” It refers to vocal music or the act of expressing words through song. The word appears once in the LXX corpus represented here, in 4 Maccabees 15:21. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, its precise role in that verse must be understood from its context. Its basic meaning remains the use of the voice in singing or chanting.

This adjective means “little” or “small,” describing something as limited in size or extent rather than large. It can describe people, objects, amounts, or other things, with the surrounding sentence showing what is being measured or contrasted. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 152 times, so it is a widely used ordinary description rather than a rare or specialized term.

This noun means “number of ten thousand,” referring to a very large counted quantity. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Wisdom 12:22. The word itself identifies the size of a number rather than describing a person, action, or quality. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains a numerical amount of ten thousand.

This proper name refers to the Moabites, the people associated with Moab. It identifies a people group rather than an action, quality, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs ten times across ten verses, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, and Deuteronomy. Its meaning remains a people designation; the specific significance of any occurrence depends on the surrounding passage. The gloss also preserves the related form “Moavitis.”

Naoum, also rendered Naum, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, in Nehemiah and Nahum. Because it functions as a personal name, its basic role is to identify a person in the passage where it occurs. The surrounding verse is needed to determine which person is being named in each occurrence.

Nebrod is a proper name—the Greek Old Testament form of the name Nebrōd or Nevroth. It identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears four times in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis, 1 Chronicles, and Micah. Its exact significance in any individual passage must be understood from that passage’s surrounding text, but the word itself functions as a personal name.

This noun means “admonition” or “warning”: a serious word of guidance intended to caution or correct someone. It names the act or message of urging a person toward a wiser or safer course, rather than merely offering casual advice. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, in Proverbs 2:2. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so its precise force in that passage must be understood from the context of Proverbs 2. Its basic sense remains a corrective warning or earnest instruction.

This adjective describes someone or something that is “carrying on the back.” It identifies a person, animal, or object by what is being carried and how it is carried, rather than naming the load itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Chronicles. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains a back-bearer or something borne on the back.

Ousa, also rendered Usa, is a proper name used to identify a person or place in the Greek Old Testament and related Jewish writings. It is not presented here as a general descriptive word with a broader everyday meaning. This name occurs 17 times in the Greek Septuagint corpus, across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise identity in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This noun names a small unit of length: “palm’s breadth; four inches.” It refers to the width of a person’s palm and is used as a practical measurement. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times across seven verses, including descriptions of objects, structures, and measured spaces. Its meaning remains a straightforward physical measurement rather than a figurative quality or action. The exact object being measured depends on the verse, but the basic sense is a palm-width, approximately four inches.

This Greek LXX verb means “beg” or “decline.” It describes asking earnestly for something, or refusing, avoiding, or excusing oneself from a request or obligation. The surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is on an appeal or a refusal. It occurs eight times in the Greek LXX corpus, in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is consistent while its exact force depends on how the verb is used in each passage.

This noun means “offshoot”: a growth that springs from a larger plant or tree. It is used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings for something that grows out from, and remains connected to, its source. The word occurs five times in this LXX corpus, including four Old Testament passages and one passage in 4 Maccabees. Its plant-based sense can be understood plainly even when the surrounding verse determines how the image is being applied.

This word asks or indicates how big or great something is. It functions as a descriptive word, drawing attention to size, extent, or degree rather than naming the thing itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, it occurs three times, including two occurrences in Zechariah and one in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what is being measured or described there.

This word means “often”: it describes something that happens repeatedly or on many occasions rather than just once. As an adverb, it modifies an action or statement by indicating how regularly it occurs. In this Greek LXX corpus, it appears nine times across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense remains consistent wherever it is used. The surrounding verse determines what action or circumstance occurs often, but the word itself emphasizes repeated frequency.

This adverb means “forward” or “far away,” describing distance or movement away from a point. It can indicate being physically distant, moving onward, or standing at a distance. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings, it occurs 17 times, so its basic sense is consistent while the surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is distance or direction. It appears in passages from 2 Chronicles, Job, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Sirach, and other books.

This Greek LXX verb means “step ahead; advance,” describing movement or progress that goes forward. It can refer to someone moving onward, or to circumstances progressing as time or events move ahead. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, across 15 verses. Its precise emphasis in any individual passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains forward movement, development, or advancement rather than staying in the same position.

This Greek LXX verb means “come before” or “go ahead.” It describes moving in front of someone or something, or proceeding ahead. The same basic idea can be rendered as coming forward in a passage. It occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including Genesis, Esther, Proverbs, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on who is moving and what or whom they precede.

This Greek LXX verb means “sit down”: it describes taking a seated position. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 5:1. That single occurrence establishes its basic lexical sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain why the person sits or what the action signifies there.

This word means “sneezing,” referring to the act or sound of sneezing. It is a noun, naming an observable bodily action rather than describing a person or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Job 41:10. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains straightforward: sneezing. The English rendering agrees with this direct sense.

Rages is a noun used as a distinct name or designation. The word does not describe an action, quality, or emotion; it identifies something called “Rages.” In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Exodus 28:32. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, the word’s precise referent in that passage cannot be described further, but its basic lexical meaning is the name “Rages.”

This noun refers to a “cleft”—a split or narrow opening in something. It names a physical feature rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs three times, in Leviticus and Isaiah. The surrounding verse determines what object or setting the cleft belongs to, but the word itself supplies the basic image of a divided or opened place.

Sabee, also rendered Savee, is a proper name referring to a person rather than describing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs eight times, all within 2 Samuel 20. Because it is a personal name, its meaning is chiefly its identifying function: it distinguishes this individual from other people in the narrative. The surrounding passage is needed to explain the person’s particular role, since the name itself does not express a virtue, action, or spiritual quality.

“Samoui; Samoi” is a proper name referring to an individual named in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal designation rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Nehemiah 11:17. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, the available information identifies the name and its location but does not establish further details about the person or the significance of the mention.

This Greek LXX noun means a “signal” or “mark”—something that indicates, identifies, or draws attention to a matter. It can describe a visible sign used to recognize a condition or distinguish something, and it can also refer to an identifying indication. The word occurs 24 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus, especially in Leviticus and Numbers, where marks and signs help identify conditions or designated times. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This LXX Greek noun means “shadow” or “shade”—a darker area formed when light is blocked, or the covering and shelter associated with such a place. It can describe an actual shadow, while its broader use may present shade as a fitting picture of obscurity or protection; the precise force depends on the surrounding verse. This word occurs 52 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, with especially frequent use in Psalms and Job. Its primary meaning and lexical identity are recorded here.

“Souba” or “Suva” is a proper name used in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The form appears twelve times in the LXX, across twelve verses. Its precise referent must be determined from the passage in which it appears. The available lexical sense is limited to these name forms; no broader ordinary-word meaning is established here.

This noun refers to a band or company—a group gathered or organized together. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs ten times, showing that it can describe a collective body rather than an individual person. Its basic sense remains broad: a band may be understood as a company of people acting or appearing together. The surrounding verse determines the particular kind of group intended in each occurrence.

This word means “distress,” describing a condition of distress experienced by people or communities. It can function as a noun, naming that condition, and its meaning remains focused on distress rather than on a person, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs 13 times across several books, including Deuteronomy, Esther, Isaiah, and the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage.

This verb means to be content with something or to consent to it. It describes agreement or willing approval rather than mere awareness of what is happening. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in the books of 1 and 2 Maccabees. Depending on the sentence, it may be rendered as agreeing, approving, or consenting, while keeping the central idea of accepting something willingly.

This noun means “sister-in-law,” referring to a woman related through marriage. It identifies a family relationship rather than an action, quality, or spiritual condition. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice, both times in one verse in Ruth. The word’s basic meaning is therefore specific and relational: a woman who is connected to someone as a sister through marriage. Its exact significance in Ruth 1:15 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This LXX noun means “hammer,” a tool used for striking. It refers to an instrument rather than an action or quality. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scripture corpus represented here, including passages from Judges, 1 Kings, Job, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its use includes ordinary tools associated with driving, shaping, or fastening objects, while the precise force in any particular verse depends on that passage’s wording and context.

Somanitis is a proper name identifying a person or people associated with that name in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general quality, action, or concept, but as a personal designation. The name occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in 1 Kings and 2 Kings. Its exact reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being discussed there.

This adjective describes something complete, whole, or accomplished. It can characterize a person or thing that meets the intended standard rather than being lacking or unfinished. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books, it occurs 19 times, showing use across descriptions of people, offerings, and wholehearted devotion. Its precise emphasis in any passage depends on what is being described, but the central idea remains completeness or full attainment.

This Greek LXX verb means to “perform” or “finish”—to carry something out or bring it to completion. It can describe completing an action, fulfilling an undertaking, or reaching the end of a task, with the surrounding sentence showing which sense is intended. The word occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented in this LXX corpus. Its basic idea remains completion: something is done, accomplished, or brought to its intended end.

This word describes something worked in relief or engraved, referring to an object shaped or decorated by carving or raised design. It functions as an adjective, so it describes the character or workmanship of a thing rather than naming the action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Kings 10:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is skilled ornamental work produced by engraving or relief carving.

e.t: This word refers to being outdoors, “in the open air,” rather than inside a building. It can function as an adjective describing an outdoor place or setting, and also as a noun for the open air itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Proverbs and once in 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense is simple and practical—something situated under the open sky or taking place outside.

This word means “suspicion”: a thought that someone or something may be dangerous, wrong, or untrustworthy, even when the matter is not yet certain. It is a noun, so it names that inward judgment or concern rather than an action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs four times—three in Daniel and once in Sirach. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation.

Phesē, also rendered Fesi, is a proper name referring to a person named in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs once in the Greek text, at Nehemiah 7:51, and its precise significance is limited to identifying that person. The available lexical information does not provide a broader meaning or word-picture beyond the personal name itself.

Phoros, also rendered Foros, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as a personal designation in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings. This name occurs 42 times in the LXX corpus, across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact reference in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and context. The form is found in passages from Joshua, Judges, Kings, Ezra, Nehemiah, and 1 Maccabees.

Chaseleu, also called Khaselev, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or person. It identifies a named term preserved in the Greek Old Testament and related writings. The form appears seven times in the Greek LXX corpus, with one occurrence in Zechariah and six in 1–2 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the lexical meaning supplied for the name is simply “Chaseleu” or “Khaselev.”

This noun means “skin,” the outer covering of a person or body. It names the visible bodily surface rather than an inner part. In the LXX corpus, including its deuterocanonical writings, it occurs four times, so its basic sense is focused and consistent. The surrounding verse determines whether the word points to someone’s bodily appearance or to skin as a physical surface.

This verb means to embank with earthen mounds—to build up earth into raised defenses or barriers. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 11:13. The word’s basic sense is therefore specific and practical: forming protective earthworks around or near a place. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly how that action functions there.
